anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Composite anomaly definition: The database simultaneously suffers from runaway accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions and from saturation or instability of the network / connection-handling layer, so that internal storage-management pressure and external communication bottlenecks coexist and interact to degrade OLTP throughput and availability.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Administrators observe ballooning table and index sizes, escalating autovacuum or purge backlogs, and steadily worsening sequential-scan times while, at the same moments, clients experience slow or failed connection attempts, intermittent time-outs, and prolonged fetch latencies. Backend processes pile up in client-read or client-write waits, yet overall transaction throughput drops because statements also spend more time traversing bloated heaps and indexes. Listener queues fill, socket counts spike with half-open or idle connections holding old snapshots, and version-store wrap-around alarms coexist with operating-system warnings about exhausted file descriptors or TCP retransmissions. The mixed symptoms can obscure root-cause isolation because server-side I/O amplification mimics network slowness, while network stalls extend transaction lifetimes and hide version-bloat effects until space or XID horizons are suddenly reached.

Causal interaction: Network congestion or connection-pool exhaustion delays transaction commit/close messages, leaving sessions in long-running states that keep their old snapshots alive. These snapshots hold back the global xmin or equivalent reclaim horizon, preventing vacuum/purge workers from removing dead tuples and deleted index entries. As obsolete versions accumulate, on-disk and in-cache data structures grow, increasing the work each query must perform and lengthening result-set transmission times. Larger result sets and slower scans in turn prolong client/network usage per transaction, further stressing listener backlogs, socket buffers, and bandwidth, creating a positive feedback loop that amplifies both anomalies and accelerates resource exhaustion. Ultimately, the intertwined issues can culminate in transaction-ID wraparound risks, critical disk-space pressure, widespread connection failures, and severe OLTP service degradation.

entry.official_definition: Write timeout for X Plugin network communication.
entry.trigger_condition: A MySQL X Protocol write operation exceeds mysqlx_write_timeout.
entry.workload_impact: The X Protocol network write operation times out.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL X Plugin system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when network data is not acknowledged, received, or written within the configured transport-level waiting window.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect packet loss, transport latency, client responsiveness, proxy behavior, and whether slow consumers or unstable links are delaying network progress.
